questions.prompt: For `struct S { char c; int i; };` on x86-64, how do the object representation and the value representation compare?
options: Object representation is all 8 bytes of storage; value representation is the 5 bytes that actually carry the value, the other 3 being padding.
Object representation is the 5 value-carrying bytes; value representation is all 8 bytes including padding.
Both are 8 bytes, since padding bytes are part of the value once the object has been initialized.
Both are 5 bytes, because `sizeof` reports only the bytes that participate in the value.
questions.explanation: Object representation is the full `sizeof(T)` sequence of `unsigned char`; value representation is the subset of bits determining the value. They diverge exactly by padding. The tempting 'both are 8' answer treats padding as value-carrying — it is not, and that is precisely why `memcmp` on this struct is unreliable.

questions.prompt: After a bad `memcpy` leaves a `bool b` with the object representation `0x02`, why can `b && !b` evaluate to true?
options: `bool` has one value bit and seven padding bits, so `0x02` is not a valid value at all and reading it is UB — the compiler may test different bits in different places.
`bool` is promoted to `int` in each operand, and `0x02` promotes to 2 in one operand and to 0 in the other.
`bool` is one byte, so `0x02` is simply `true`, and `!b` is `false`; the expression is short-circuited into being true.
`bool` objects are stored as bitfields, so two adjacent `bool`s can share a byte and corrupt each other's bit.
questions.explanation: The storage is a byte but only one bit is a value bit, so `0x02` corresponds to no value of the type and the read is undefined. The promotion answer is tempting because promotion really does happen, but promotion of a valid `bool` is deterministic — the anomaly comes from the invalid representation, not from conversion rules.

questions.prompt: Which claim about reading a struct's padding bytes is correct?
options: Reading padding through `unsigned char` or `std::byte` yields an unspecified value; reading it as part of the member's own type would be undefined behavior.
Reading padding through any pointer type is fine, since padding is merely unspecified rather than indeterminate.
Reading padding is undefined behavior through every pointer type, including `unsigned char` and `std::byte`.
Reading padding is defined only after the struct has been value-initialized with `= {}`, which zeroes it.
questions.explanation: Indeterminate values are UB to read, with the single carve-out for `unsigned char`/`std::byte`, which yields an unspecified value instead. The '`= {}` zeroes padding' answer is the widespread misconception: `= {}` zeroes members, not padding, so value-initialization does not launder the indeterminacy away.

questions.prompt: A lock-free queue uses `std::atomic<Node>::compare_exchange_strong` where `Node` has internal padding. What is the characteristic failure?
options: The CAS can spin forever because it compares object representations, so differing padding makes the comparison fail even when all member values match.
The CAS silently succeeds when values differ, because padding bytes are masked out of the comparison before it runs.
The compiler rejects the code, because `std::atomic<T>` requires `has_unique_object_representations_v<T>` to be true.
The CAS tears, writing half the members, because a padded struct cannot be stored with a single instruction.
questions.explanation: CAS is a byte-wise comparison of the object representation, so garbage padding in the expected value never matches and the loop never terminates. The 'requires unique object representations' answer is the near-miss: `atomic<T>` requires only *trivially copyable*, not unique object representations, so a padded type compiles fine and fails at runtime. Fix by adding explicit padding members or CASing an integer.

questions.prompt: Which trait is the precise answer to "may I `memcmp` and byte-hash this type?"
options: `std::has_unique_object_representations_v<T>` — true only when the type has no padding bits and equal values always share one representation.
`std::is_trivially_copyable_v<T>` — true when `memcpy` of the bytes preserves the value, which is the same requirement.
`std::is_standard_layout_v<T>` — true when member offsets are predictable, which fixes the padding question.
`std::is_pod_v<T>` — the conjunction of triviality and standard layout, which together rule padding out.
questions.explanation: Only `has_unique_object_representations_v` speaks about padding bits and representation uniqueness. Trivial copyability is the seductive wrong answer: `struct S { char c; int i; };` is trivially copyable yet full of padding, so `memcpy` is safe while `memcmp` is not. Note the trait is also false for anything containing `float`/`double`, since `+0.0` and `-0.0` compare equal with different bytes.

questions.prompt: Why is `sizeof(T)` always required to be a multiple of `alignof(T)`?
options: So that array elements stay aligned: `T arr[N]` is contiguous with no gaps, so every element's address must remain a multiple of the alignment.
So that `alignof(T)` can be computed from `sizeof(T)` by rounding down to the nearest power of two.
So that `memcpy` of a whole object can always use the widest available load and store instructions.
So that the compiler can place any object of type `T` at the start of a cache line without extra work.
questions.explanation: Arrays are contiguous, so element `i` sits at `base + i * sizeof(T)`; only a size that is a multiple of the alignment keeps every element aligned. This is exactly what forces tail padding, making `struct { int; char; }` 8 rather than 5. The `memcpy` answer is a real-sounding benefit but not the reason — wide copies are legal regardless of the size relation.

questions.prompt: Two threads each increment their own `std::atomic<uint64_t>`, and the two counters are adjacent members of one struct. Throughput collapses. What is happening and what fixes it?
options: False sharing: the counters share a cache line and MESI ping-pongs it between cores; separate them with `alignas(64)` on each.
A split lock: each atomic RMW straddles a cache line and asserts a bus lock; fix it by shrinking the counters to 32 bits.
Lock-table contention: `atomic<uint64_t>` is not lock-free, so both threads serialize on one library mutex; fix it with a plain `uint64_t`.
Store buffering: each core stalls draining its store buffer; fix it by relaxing the memory order on both increments.
questions.explanation: Independent variables on one 64-byte line cause each write to invalidate the other core's copy, serializing logically independent work at roughly 100ns per operation. The split-lock distractor describes a different pathology — that requires an atomic that *straddles* a line boundary, whereas here each atomic is perfectly aligned and merely shares a line with its neighbour.

questions.prompt: Which statement about `alignas` and packing is correct?
options: `alignas` can only strengthen alignment — `alignas(1) int` is ill-formed — so removing padding requires `#pragma pack` or `[[gnu::packed]]`.
`alignas` can both strengthen and weaken alignment, making `#pragma pack` merely a non-portable spelling of `alignas(1)`.
`alignas` weakens alignment on members but strengthens it on whole classes, which is why packed structs mix the two.
`alignas` affects only the address the object is placed at, never `sizeof`, so a packed struct and an aligned one match in size.
questions.explanation: The standard permits strengthening only; a weaker request is ill-formed, which is why packing is a compiler extension rather than a language feature. The 'alignment never affects `sizeof`' answer is subtly wrong in a common way: `alignas(64)` on a class rounds `sizeof` up to 64 too, because size must stay a multiple of alignment.

questions.prompt: Code takes `&packed.field` on a `[[gnu::packed]]` struct, passes the pointer to a helper, and dereferences it. It works on x86-64 and crashes on ARM. What is the correct assessment?
options: The pointer may be misaligned, and dereferencing a misaligned pointer is UB regardless of platform — x86 tolerance is luck, not licence; `memcpy` the field out instead.
It is legal C++ on both platforms; the ARM crash is a toolchain bug and `-mno-unaligned-access` is the correct workaround.
It is UB only on ARM, since UB is defined relative to the target ABI and x86-64 documents misaligned loads as supported.
The problem is the packed attribute changing `sizeof`, so the helper reads past the end of the struct on ARM's larger layout.
questions.explanation: Misaligned access is UB in C++ everywhere; the compiler is entitled to assume alignment and emit aligned SIMD, so 'x86 allows it' is not a defense. GCC flags this with `-Waddress-of-packed-member`. The 'UB only on ARM' answer is the popular rationalization — UB is a property of the abstract machine, not of what a given CPU happens to tolerate.

questions.prompt: What does `struct Bad { char a; double b; char c; int d; };` occupy, and what does reordering buy?
options: 24 bytes; declaring `double b; int d; char a; char c;` gives 16 bytes, cutting waste from 11 bytes to 2.
16 bytes; reordering cannot help, because the compiler already sorts members by decreasing alignment internally.
14 bytes; reordering to 16 bytes actually costs space but improves the alignment of the `double`.
24 bytes; reordering gives 14 bytes, since removing all holes leaves exactly the sum of the member sizes.
questions.explanation: Laying out in order gives a[1] pad[7] b[8] c[1] pad[3] d[4] = 24; sorting by decreasing alignment gives b[8] d[4] a[1] c[1] pad[2] = 16. The 'reordering gives 14 bytes' answer is the natural off-by-a-concept: the members sum to 14, but tail padding must round the size up to a multiple of `alignof` (8), so 16 is the floor, not 14.

questions.prompt: Given `struct Base { int i; char c; };` and `struct Derived : Base { char d; };`, what is `sizeof(Derived)` on the Itanium ABI and why?
options: 8 — `d` is placed into `Base`'s tail padding, which the ABI may reuse because `Base` is not standard-layout as a subobject here.
12 — `Base` contributes its full 8 bytes and `d` plus tail padding adds another 4, since padding is never reused.
16 — the derived object must be aligned to twice the base's alignment to keep the subobject addressable.
8 — the compiler reorders `d` before `c` to fill the hole, which is permitted across access-control sections.
questions.explanation: Tail padding of a non-standard-layout base subobject is available to the derived class, so `d` lands at offset 5 and the size stays 8. The 'compiler reorders `d` before `c`' answer reaches the right number by the wrong mechanism — C++ never reorders members to save space; the saving comes purely from reuse. The practical hazard is that `memcpy`ing `sizeof(Base)` bytes over a `Derived` now clobbers `d`.

questions.prompt: For `struct Empty {}; struct A { Empty e; int i; }; struct B : Empty { int i; };`, what are the sizes?
options: `sizeof(A) == 8` and `sizeof(B) == 4` — an empty member needs a distinct address, but an empty base can occupy zero bytes.
`sizeof(A) == 4` and `sizeof(B) == 4` — both empty subobjects are elided, since `Empty` has no members to store.
`sizeof(A) == 8` and `sizeof(B) == 8` — the base subobject also needs a distinct address from the derived object.
`sizeof(A) == 5` and `sizeof(B) == 4` — the empty member costs one byte and no padding is inserted after it.
questions.explanation: An empty *member* must have a unique address, so it takes a byte plus 3 bytes of padding before the `int`; the Empty Base Optimization lets an empty *base* take none. The '`sizeof(A) == 5`' answer gets the member cost right but forgets alignment: `i` must land at offset 4, so `A` is 8, not 5. C++20's `[[no_unique_address]]` brings the base behaviour to members.

questions.prompt: Given `struct Flags { unsigned a : 1; unsigned b : 3; };`, one thread writes `f.a` while another writes `f.b`, with no synchronization. What is the verdict?
options: A data race — adjacent bit-fields form a single memory location; inserting `unsigned : 0;` between them would separate the locations.
Well-defined — the memory model treats each named bit-field as its own memory location precisely to allow this pattern.
A data race only on big-endian targets, where the bit allocation order places both fields in the same byte.
Well-defined provided both writes are through `volatile` bit-fields, which forces read-modify-write to be atomic.
questions.explanation: Adjacent bit-fields with no zero-width field between them are one memory location, so concurrent writes race even though the fields are logically independent — the read-modify-write of the storage unit clobbers the neighbour. The `volatile` answer is a common misconception: `volatile` orders nothing and provides no atomicity in the C++ memory model.

questions.prompt: Which of these is trivially copyable but **not** trivially default constructible?
options: `struct B { int x = 0; };` — the NSDMI kills trivial default construction while leaving copying trivial.
`struct C { C(const C&) {} int x; };` — the user-provided copy constructor blocks default construction.
`struct E { virtual void f(); };` — the vptr must be initialized, which makes both operations non-trivial.
`struct D { std::string s; };` — the member's own constructor makes the aggregate non-trivial throughout.
questions.explanation: An in-class initializer means the default constructor has work to do, but it says nothing about copying, so `B` remains trivially copyable. `C` is the mirror image and the tempting swap — a user-provided copy constructor destroys trivial *copyability* while its implicit default constructor stays trivial. Conflating these two axes is one of the chapter's named traps.

questions.prompt: Why can adding a destructor to an 8-byte type make calls slower under the SysV ABI?
options: It stops being trivially copyable, so the type must be passed by invisible reference in memory rather than in a register.
The destructor call itself is emitted at every call site, and the call overhead dominates for such a small type.
The type stops being standard-layout, so the ABI can no longer compute a stable offset for its single member.
The type gains a hidden vtable pointer for destructor dispatch, doubling its size from 8 bytes to 16.
questions.explanation: Register passing is available only to trivially copyable types; a non-trivial destructor forces memory passing even for a tiny type — which is why `unique_ptr` is not zero-overhead at ABI boundaries despite being pointer-sized. The vtable answer is wrong on its face: only *virtual* functions add a vptr, and a plain destructor adds nothing to the layout.

questions.prompt: How do trivial copyability and trivial relocatability relate?
options: Trivial copyability implies trivial relocatability, but not the converse — an SSO `std::string` is relocatable yet not trivially copyable.
Trivial relocatability implies trivial copyability, but not the converse — relocation is the strictly stronger byte-level guarantee.
Neither implies the other — a self-referential intrusive-list node is trivially copyable but never trivially relocatable.
They are one property under two names, and C++26 merely renames the existing trait for clarity.
questions.explanation: The implication runs one way only: anything `memcpy` preserves can also be moved-and-destroyed by `memcpy`, so trivially copyable types are relocatable. The converse fails, which is the whole reason P1144/P2786 needed a separate trait — relocation is move-plus-destroy-source, which an SSO string satisfies despite its interior pointer making byte copies invalid. The reversed-implication option is the tempting one precisely because relocation *sounds* like the stronger property.

questions.prompt: Which class is **not** standard-layout?
options: `struct NSL { public: int a; private: int b; };` — non-static data members with different access control.
`struct F { F(int) {} int x; };` — a user-provided constructor prevents predictable member offsets.
`struct G { int x = 0; int y; };` — an in-class initializer disqualifies the aggregate.
`struct SLd : SL { };` — a derived class always splits data across the hierarchy.
questions.explanation: Standard layout requires all non-static data members to share one access control, so mixing `public` and `private` disqualifies `NSL`. The constructor and NSDMI options are the classic confusion with *triviality*: user-provided constructors and in-class initializers cost triviality, not standard layout. And `SLd` is fine because all the data still lives in exactly one class of the chain.

questions.prompt: What is the modern answer to "what is a POD type?"
options: An obsolete conjunction of trivial and standard-layout, deprecated in C++20 — ask instead which property is needed: `memcpy`-ability or predictable offsets.
A type with no constructors, destructors, or virtual functions, which C++20 renamed to 'aggregate' without changing the meaning.
A synonym for trivially copyable, since byte-copyability was always the property the term was reaching for.
A type whose members are all fundamental types, which is why `std::is_pod` was replaced by concept-based checks.
questions.explanation: POD bundled two orthogonal properties, which is why `std::is_pod` was deprecated in favour of `is_trivially_copyable` and `is_standard_layout`. The 'synonym for trivially copyable' answer is the most tempting since that is the property people usually want, but POD was strictly stronger — it also demanded standard layout, and aggregates are a third, unrelated notion.

questions.prompt: Before C++20, why was `void* buf = malloc(sizeof(int)); *static_cast<int*>(buf) = 42;` formally undefined?
options: There was storage but no `int` *object* had ever been created there, and you may not access an object that does not exist.
`malloc` returns memory aligned only for `char`, so the store to an `int` was a misaligned access.
`static_cast` from `void*` to `int*` was itself ill-formed without an intervening `reinterpret_cast`.
Writing through a pointer obtained from a C library function violated strict aliasing, since `malloc` returns `void*`.
questions.explanation: Lifetime formally begins when an object is created, and nothing in that snippet created one — which meant allocators, ring buffers, deserializers, and `std::vector` itself were all technically UB. C++20's implicit object creation (P0593) made `malloc` create the `int`. The alignment answer is wrong on the facts: `malloc` returns storage suitably aligned for any object of fundamental alignment.

questions.prompt: You `read()` a `Header`'s bytes into a `char buf[sizeof(Header)]` and want to access them as a `Header` without copying. What is the C++23 tool and what does it cost?
options: `std::start_lifetime_as<Header>(buf)` — it emits no code, simply declaring to the abstract machine that those bytes are a `Header`.
`std::bit_cast<Header>(buf)` — it emits no code and reinterprets the buffer in place with no object created.
`std::launder(reinterpret_cast<Header*>(buf))` — it refreshes the pointer so the bytes become a valid `Header`.
Placement `new (buf) Header{}` — it costs nothing for an implicit-lifetime type and formally creates the object.
questions.explanation: `start_lifetime_as` is exactly the zero-code declaration that existing bytes are an object, needed because `read()` is not one of the implicitly-creating operations. `bit_cast` is the tempting near-miss: it does produce a `Header`, but by *copying* the bytes into a new object rather than adopting them in place. `launder` only refreshes a pointer to an object that already exists, and placement `new` overwrites the bytes you just read.

questions.prompt: Which operation does **not** implicitly create objects of implicit-lifetime types in the storage it touches?
options: `std::launder`, which only refreshes an existing pointer and creates nothing.
`std::memmove` into a region, which implicitly creates the objects that make the program well-defined.
`std::allocator::allocate`, which implicitly creates objects in the storage it returns.
`std::bit_cast`, which implicitly creates the destination object from the source bytes.
questions.explanation: The implicitly-creating set is the allocation functions, `memcpy`/`memmove`, `bit_cast`, and beginning the lifetime of a `unsigned char`/`std::byte` array. `launder` is not in it — it presupposes an object already exists at the address and merely defeats the compiler's assumption that it is still the *old* one, which is why it cannot rescue a `reinterpret_cast` over foreign bytes.

questions.prompt: Why does the classic `float fast_inv_sqrt` written with `int i = *(int*)&x;` produce wrong results at `-O2`?
options: Accessing a `float` through an `int` lvalue is UB, and the optimizer assumes `int*` and `float*` never alias, so it keeps stale values in registers.
The `int` and `float` have different alignments, so the reinterpreted load reads from a shifted address at higher optimization levels.
The magic constant depends on a specific FPU rounding mode that `-O2` changes by enabling fast-math transformations.
The compiler narrows the `float` to `int` with a value conversion instead of a bit reinterpretation once inlining exposes the cast.
questions.explanation: Strict aliasing lets the compiler assume a store through `float*` cannot affect a value loaded through `int*`, so the reads and writes get reordered or elided. The 'narrowing value conversion' answer describes what a `static_cast` would do, not a `reinterpret_cast` — the cast really does reinterpret bits; the breakage is the optimizer's aliasing assumption, not a conversion. `std::bit_cast` or `memcpy` is the correct spelling.

questions.prompt: What is the status of union-based type punning?
options: Legal in C, formally UB in C++, but documented as a supported extension by GCC, Clang, and MSVC.
Legal in both C and C++ since C++11, when the standard adopted C's active-member reading rules.
UB in C and in C++, which is why the common initial sequence rule was added to cover the safe cases.
Legal in C++ but UB in C, which is why C code uses `memcpy` and C++ code uses unions for punning.
questions.explanation: C explicitly blesses reading a non-active member; C++ never adopted that and the read is UB, though the major compilers document it as working. The 'UB in both C and C++' answer overstates the case in a plausible way: the common initial sequence rule is real but far narrower — it only licenses reading *shared leading members* of layout-compatible standard-layout structs, not arbitrary reinterpretation.

questions.prompt: The chapter says the `char*` aliasing exemption is "one-directional." What does that mean concretely?
options: You may read any object's bytes through `char*`, but you may not take a `char` array and read it as an `int` — that needs `start_lifetime_as` or a copy.
You may write any object's bytes through `char*`, but reading them back requires the object's own type to refresh the value.
You may alias through `unsigned char*` but not through `char*`, since only the unsigned variant appears in the representation wording.
You may alias a `char` array as any type, but you may not alias a non-`char` object through `char*` without `std::launder`.
questions.explanation: The exemption lets a `char`/`unsigned char`/`std::byte` glvalue access any object, but it grants nothing in the reverse direction: raw bytes do not become an `int` object just because you point an `int*` at them. The 'a `char` array may be aliased as any type' answer inverts the rule exactly, which is why it reads convincingly — it is the direction that actually requires the C++23 lifetime tool.

questions.prompt: For a big-endian wire protocol, why is the shift-based `read_u32_be` preferred over `ntohl(*(uint32_t*)p)`?
options: The shift form is endianness-independent by construction and needs no aliasing violation or aligned load, yet still folds to one `BSWAP`.
The shift form is faster because `ntohl` is a library call that cannot be inlined and costs a function call per field.
The shift form works on 64-bit values, whereas `ntohl` is limited to 16-bit quantities on every POSIX platform.
The shift form zero-extends correctly, whereas `ntohl` sign-extends its result on big-endian hosts.
questions.explanation: Indexing bytes and shifting never consults the host's byte order, so no `#ifdef` is needed, and it avoids both the strict-aliasing violation of the cast and the possibly misaligned load — while compilers still fold it to a load plus `BSWAP`. The performance answer is wrong on its premise: `ntohl` is typically a macro or intrinsic, so speed is not the differentiator; correctness is.

questions.prompt: A bit-field struct that parses a protocol header correctly on x86-64 is recompiled for a big-endian target and misparses. Why?
options: Bit allocation order within a storage unit is ABI-defined — LSB-first on x86 SysV, MSB-first elsewhere — so the fields land on different bits.
Byte order changed but bit order did not, so only fields that straddle a byte boundary are affected, and only in the widest field.
The struct's tail padding moved, shifting every field by the size of the padding introduced at the end.
Bit-fields are always MSB-first by the standard, so only the surrounding non-bit-field members were affected by the endian change.
questions.explanation: Almost everything about bit-fields is implementation-defined, including which end of the storage unit allocation starts from, so the same declarations map to different bits under a different ABI. The 'bit-fields are always MSB-first' answer is the confident-sounding falsehood: the standard fixes no allocation order at all, which is exactly why the chapter says never to use bit-fields for wire formats.

questions.prompt: `int a[10], b[10];` with `int* p = a + 10;` and `int* q = b;`. At runtime `p == q` is true. Is `*p = 1;` legal?
options: No — `p`'s provenance is the array `a`, so it may only access `a`, regardless of the address it happens to hold.
Yes — once two pointers compare equal they denote the same object, so either may be used to access it.
Yes, but only if the write goes through `q`; assigning `p = q` first would launder the provenance.
No — the comparison itself is UB, since comparing pointers into different objects has no defined result.
questions.explanation: A pointer carries an origin object as well as an address, and one-past-the-end of `a` may never be used to touch `b` even when the bit patterns match. The 'the comparison itself is UB' answer is a near-miss worth separating: relational comparison (`<`) across distinct objects is unspecified, but `==` is well-defined — the comparison is fine, it is the *access* that is not.

questions.prompt: For `int a[10];`, which pointer computation is well-defined?
options: `int* p = a + 10;` — one past the end is explicitly blessed, though dereferencing it is not.
`int* q = a + 11;` — computing an out-of-range pointer is fine as long as it is never dereferenced.
`int* r = a - 1;` — a symmetric one-before-the-beginning position exists for reverse iteration.
`int* s = a + 10;` followed by `*s = 0;` — writing to the end position is how `push_back` works.
questions.explanation: Only the one-past-the-end position is defined, and only as a value — dereferencing it is UB, which rules out writing through the end position with `*s = 0;`. The `a - 1` answer is the tempting symmetry: there is no one-before-the-beginning, which is precisely why `std::reverse_iterator` stores the *next* position and dereferences `*(it - 1)`. Merely computing `a + 11` is already undefined, no dereference required.

questions.prompt: Given `struct A { int type; int x; }; struct B { int type; double y; }; union U { A a; B b; };` with `u.a` active, what may you legally read?
options: `u.b.type` — it is in the common initial sequence of two layout-compatible standard-layout structs; `u.b.y` would be UB.
Both `u.b.type` and `u.b.y` — once the union is visible, any member of either struct may be read.
Neither — reading through a non-active union member is undefined behavior in C++ without exception.
`u.b.y` only — the shared `type` member aliases across both structs and so must be read via `u.a`.
questions.explanation: The common initial sequence is the longest run of leading members with layout-compatible types, and reading it through the inactive member is explicitly permitted when both structs are standard-layout and the union is visible. The 'neither member may be read' answer overcorrects with the general union-punning rule — that rule is real, but this carve-out is exactly what makes tagged unions and the `struct sockaddr` family legal.

questions.prompt: When is `offsetof(T, m)` well-defined, and what is its canonical use?
options: For standard-layout `T`; it underpins the `container_of` idiom that recovers an enclosing object from a member pointer in intrusive containers.
For trivially copyable `T`; it underpins `memcpy`-based field extraction from wire buffers into struct members.
For any complete `T`; it underpins the vtable-offset arithmetic that virtual inheritance uses to find base subobjects.
For aggregate `T` only; it underpins aggregate initialization by giving each initializer its destination offset.
questions.explanation: Standard layout is the condition that makes offsets fixed and computable, and `container_of` — subtracting the offset from a member's address — is why the macro exists, powering the Linux kernel's `list_head` and Boost.Intrusive. The 'any complete `T`, for virtual-inheritance offsets' answer is the exact inversion of the truth: virtual bases are the case where `offsetof` genuinely breaks, because a member's offset is not a compile-time constant at all.

questions.prompt: Which single `static_assert` most directly guarantees a wire struct has no padding anywhere in it?
options: `static_assert(std::has_unique_object_representations_v<Order>);`
`static_assert(std::is_trivially_copyable_v<Order>);`
`static_assert(std::is_standard_layout_v<Order>);`
`static_assert(alignof(Order) == sizeof(Order));`
questions.explanation: `has_unique_object_representations_v` is false if any padding bit exists anywhere in the type, making it the strongest single assertion in the wire-format checklist. Standard layout is the tempting choice because it is the other name in every ABI discussion, but it fixes member *order and offsets* while saying nothing about holes between them — a standard-layout struct can be mostly padding.

questions.prompt: A team places `std::atomic<MyStruct>` in a shared-memory segment for cross-process synchronization. What is the hidden failure?
options: If it is not `is_always_lock_free`, the implementation uses a process-local lock table, so there is no cross-process atomicity at all.
Atomics require page alignment in shared memory, so mapping the segment at a different base address breaks the alignment guarantee.
`std::atomic` stores a vtable pointer for its lock strategy, which is only valid in the writing process's address space.
The atomic operations succeed but the memory ordering is downgraded to relaxed, since fences do not propagate across processes.
questions.explanation: Non-lock-free atomics fall back to a table of mutexes inside the process, so each process locks a different mutex and the operations are not mutually atomic — silently. `static_assert(std::atomic<T>::is_always_lock_free)` is mandatory here. The 'atomic stores a vtable pointer' answer invents a vtable: `std::atomic` has no virtual functions; the process-local state lives in the library's lock table, not in the object.
